contexts.stem: You look exhausted — you ___ get some rest before the trip. (advice)
She has a bad cough; she ___ see a doctor soon.
It's raining hard — we ___ take an umbrella.
After should, the verb has no extra word: you should ___ more water. (drink)
He hurt his friend, so he ___ to apologise. (use the formal modal with 'to')
After 'ought', the little word ___ is always needed: you ought ___ go.
You ___ smoke in here — it isn't allowed. (negative advice)
___ I open the window? It's a bit warm. (ask for advice, modal first)
The train ___ arrive at ten — that's the timetable. (expectation)
What ___ we do about the broken printer? (ask for advice)
You really ___ try this restaurant; the pasta is excellent. (recommendation)
Children ___ be rude to their teachers. (negative advice)
She finishes work at six, so she ___ be home by now. (reasonable expectation)
The bus ___ be here in five minutes — it's usually on time. (expectation, not advice)
I'm not certain, but I think you ___ apologise. (softened advice)
Maybe you ___ ask her directly instead of guessing. (tentative advice)
In formal writing one ___ to weigh both sides of the argument. (formal modal with 'to')
___ we invite her too? It seems unfair to leave her out. (negative-leaning suggestion, modal first)
I don't think you ___ lend him money — he never pays it back. (negative advice on the right modal)
The formal negative of the duty modal keeps its 'to': you ___ to lie on the form. (ought + negative)
___ I carry that bag for you? (offer to help, not asking for advice)
He's been travelling all day, so he ___ be quite tired by now — though I'm not sure. (weaker than 'must')
I ___ called her yesterday, but I completely forgot. (regret about the past)
You ___ told me the meeting was cancelled! I waited an hour. (criticism of the past)
We ___ stayed so late — now everyone is exhausted. (regret, negative)
In writing, never use 'should of'; the correct form is should ___ . (fill the missing word)
After 'have' you need the past participle: she should have ___ . (go)
The parcel ___ arrived by now, but it still hasn't. (unmet expectation in the past)
It's the formal equivalent: she ___ to have apologised at once. (ought + perfect)
___ you require assistance, please call reception. (formal inverted conditional, no 'if')
Applicants ___ submit their CV by Friday — softer than 'must' but still expected. (formal instruction)
It is important that the report ___ be checked before it is sent. (subjunctive that-clause)
She insisted that we ___ stay for dinner. (subjunctive after 'insist')
I'm checking my expectation: she ___ have arrived by now. (expectation, not a confident deduction)
I ___ think she's already left — the lights are off. (British tentative opinion, not advice)
___ any discrepancies arise, please notify us at once. (formal inverted conditional)
It is essential that all staff ___ be informed of the change. (subjunctive 'should')
He demanded that she ___ leave the building immediately. (subjunctive after 'demand')
In British academic prose, with a moral colouring, one ___ to respect the views of others. (the marked moral modal + 'to')
You ___ have been working, not playing games all afternoon. (criticism of an extended past action)
I ___ imagine the report will run to forty pages. (polite, hedged opinion — British register)
In the inverted conditional the modal moves to the front and 'if' disappears: ___ you change your mind, let me know. (rewrite of 'If you...')
After subjunctive 'should' the verb stays in the base form: he demanded that she should ___ at once. (leave)
It ___ be remembered that correlation does not imply causation. (reader-directed academic hedge)
With full moral weight and distance, one ___ not to pass judgement without the facts. (marked moral modal, negative + 'to')
___ the worst come to the worst, we still have a contingency plan. (formal inverted-conditional idiom)
He ___ to have known better than to sign without reading it. (past moral criticism, the marked modal + perfect)
And who ___ walk in at that very moment but the person we'd been discussing! (literary narrative surprise, base verb follows)
How ___ I know where he keeps his keys? (idiomatic rhetorical refusal)
Why ___ he care what they think of his decision? (rhetorical indifference)
It is hereby ordered that the defendant ___ appear on the appointed date. (subjunctive 'should' in legal register)
I ___ have thought that point was self-evident, frankly. (high-register polemical hedge)
She ___ to have realised that silence would be read as consent. (moral criticism with the marked modal + perfect)
For past moral criticism use the full form: he ought ___ have known better. (fill the missing word)
